## Most Important Thing

Deepen understanding of "good" in the context of whether it works or not; identify failure modes

## Outcomes

- Name the six failure modes, and say which lever fixes each
- Classify an observed failure into a mode and defend the classification
- Describe a failure along the three dimensions (silent/loud, isolated/cascading, model/code)
- Recognize the same failure under other names, and explain why no taxonomy is authoritative

## Notes

Start the conversation by asking what they expect from an agent, and what they would see as a
failure. Collect their answers before showing the taxonomy — the list lands better as a
tidying-up of what they already said than as a list handed down.

The taxonomy is committed in [failure_modes.md](../course_design/failure_modes.md). Teach from
that document; it is the source of truth and holds the reasoning, the dropped categories, and
the source links.

### The framing that makes it teachable

The modes are **named for the lever that fixes them**, not for the phenomenon. So this is not a
new list to memorize — it is the Module 1 build levers read backwards. Say that out loud early;
it converts the whole day from vocabulary drill into recognition.

| Mode | What went wrong | Lever |
|---|---|---|
| Tool | wrong tool, bad args, unparsed output | tool definitions & schemas |
| Grounding | asserts what nothing supports | retrieval / knowledge state |
| State | needed info lost, stale, or poisoned | state & memory design |
| Control | won't stop, stops early, wanders | deterministic scaffolding |
| Specification | did what you said, not what you meant | instructions & spec |
| Safety | harmful or disallowed, even if correct | guardrails, permissions, HITL |

Naming the mode *is* naming the fix. That is the whole point, and it is what makes the bridge
competency (root-cause → choose a lever) teachable in a single day.

### Admit the mess — out loud, early

- No authoritative taxonomy exists. Every list is cut for a different purpose.
- OWASP Top 10 for LLM Apps (2025) — cut by attacker. Mostly collapses into our Safety.
- MAST (arxiv 2503.13657) — cut by trace analysis. 14 modes, multi-agent only.
- Vendor lists — cut by what their tool detects. Five or six items, never the same six.
- Ours is cut by the lever, because our question is "what do I change?"
- Line to use: *"Six because you need to say something in a meeting Tuesday. It's a tool, not a discovery."*
- Why say it: they'll hit other lists this week, and Outcome 5 says an unhedged list in a
  four-year-old field is the warning sign.

**If they push back that OWASP is authoritative — agree, then show the cut.** It's a risk
register (what can hurt you); ours is a repair manual (what's broken, indexed by the fix). No
conflicts, because different axes. Work the mapping live:

- 4 of their 10 → our Safety alone (prompt injection, sensitive info disclosure, excessive
  agency, system prompt leakage). Our one lever, their whole field.
- 2 land outside our six (supply chain, model poisoning) — build-time, no lever a student can
  pull. Name it as a gap in ours, don't paper over it.
- Misinformation → Grounding. Unbounded consumption → Control. Improper output handling → Tool.
- **Two of ours have no OWASP entry: State and Specification.** "Forgot the order number" and
  "did what I said, not what I meant" aren't security risks — and they're most of Project 2.
- The point, sharper than "everyone disagrees": *the most authoritative list in the room is
  authoritative about a different question.*
- Detail worth using: LLM09 is "Misinformation," not "hallucination." OWASP dodged the popular
  word too.

### Aliases — recognition, not memorization

- **Tool** — tool interface / selection / execution error · parsing error · schema violation
- **Grounding** — hallucination · fabrication · confabulation · faithfulness · sycophancy
- **State** — context loss / exhaustion / degradation / rot · dumb zone · memory pollution
- **Control** — infinite loop · budget drain · runaway · planning failure · premature termination
- **Specification** — goal / semantic / spec drift · instruction decay · reward hacking
- **Safety** — alignment violation · prompt injection · jailbreak · excessive agency · exfiltration

"Hallucination" is the most-used and least useful word. Follow-up is always: *which lever?*

### The long list — hand out, don't lecture

Job: make six feel like a compression of something real, not an arbitrary short list.

Tool — parsing error · wrong tool · bad args · never called · tool errored · too many tools ·
mis-framed descriptions
Grounding — fabricated facts/citations/APIs · retrieval miss, answered anyway · retrieved and
contradicted it · sycophantic confirmation
State — window exhaustion · context degradation · memory pollution · session state loss
Control — infinite loop · budget drain · premature termination · bad plan · abandons plan ·
wanders · sub-agent coordination loss · deadlock
Specification — spec drift · semantic drift · hidden assumption · reward hacking
Safety — prompt injection · excessive agency · data leak · alignment faking

Then the payoff: **cascading errors** and **code bug** are top-level modes on published lists
and dimensions in ours. Taxonomies disagree about what counts as a category, not about what
goes wrong.

### The dimensions carry the real skill

Spend real time here, not just on the six.

- **silent ↔ loud** — trains **detection**. A stack trace is a bug report; a confidently wrong
  refund amount is a diagnosis. Ask: "how would you have caught this if it never crashed?"
  Every evaluator they write later is an answer to that question.
- **isolated ↔ cascading** — trains **localization**. Hunt the trace for the *earliest* bad
  span, not the last. This is the skill that makes their LangSmith reading from 2_2 pay off.
- **model ↔ code** — students reflexively blame the model. Separate it early.

### Coverage note

[slide2_3.qmd](../lecture_slides/slide2_3.qmd) works three of the six in depth — Control
(infinite loop), Tool (hallucinated planning), Safety (unsafe tool use). Grounding, State, and
Specification are named but not worked; students meet them in Project 2. If a day frees up,
Specification is the one most worth promoting to a worked example, since it is the hand-off to
Outcome 3.

The hallucinated-planning slide is the best demonstration of why the taxonomy is lever-named:
students want to file it under Grounding because "hallucination" sounds like a model problem,
but its fix is the tool schema. Let them make that mistake before correcting it.

### Simple outline

- Ask what they expect, what counts as failure — collect on the board
- Reveal the six, mapped back to the levers they already built
- Dimensions, with emphasis on silent and cascading
- Classify real failures from traces; make them *defend* the label
- Where classifications are contested, that's the lesson — several levers can be plausible

### Caution

Some failures genuinely admit more than one fix, so the mode is a judgment call rather than a
lookup. Do not present the taxonomy as a decision tree with unique answers. The assessable act
is defending a classification with trace evidence, not producing the "right" label.
